\chapter{Undicesimo, Prima e Dopo}
\label{ch:it-ordinali-esimo}
\hlchaptermodality{28}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can build any ordinal above ten with -esimo, put two things in order with prima and dopo, and lay out the courses of a meal in sequence.}

The ordinals and prima/dopo used on the same four things, so the difference between naming a place and naming a relation is worked rather than stated.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[undicesimo]{undicesimo — where Italian stops inheriting and starts building}

\label{lesson:IT-C28-undicesimo}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, and then the ending that ends the memorizing.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{decimo} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sesto} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{l'orecchio} — \textbf{R2}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{essere e stato} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{andare} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{io} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mi chiamo} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: take the number, drop its last vowel, add -esimo}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{undici} $\to$ \textbf{undicesimo} — eleventh. \textbf{venti} $\to$ \textbf{ventesimo} — twentieth. \textbf{cento} $\to$ \textbf{centesimo} — hundredth.
\end{quote}

Ten inherited words stopped at \emph{decimo}. Above ten, Italian built something instead: take the cardinal you already know, take its final vowel off, and put \textbf{-ésimo} on the end. That is all of it, and it runs to infinity.

Say the three above out loud and hear the number still sitting inside each one. \emph{Undicesimo} is \emph{undici} wearing a suffix; nothing has to be memorized separately.

\textbf{One word keeps its vowel}, and it is \emph{tre}: \emph{ventitré} gives \textbf{ventitreesimo}, with the \emph{e} still there. Drop it and the number would vanish from the word.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: two systems, one number line}]
So Italian numbers order in two different ways and the seam is at ten:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{range} & \textbf{how it is made} \\
\midrule
first to tenth & \textbf{ten inherited words}, each its own accident \\
eleventh upward & \textbf{cardinal minus final vowel, plus -esimo} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is worth knowing as a shape, not only as a fact. The commonest ten words in a language are the ones that survive irregular, because they are said too often to be tidied; everything past them gets built by rule, because a rule is what you reach for when the word is rare. You will meet the same seam in the verbs.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{undici $\to$ undicesimo}
  \item \emph{venti $\to$ ventesimo}
  \item \emph{ventitré $\to$ ventitreesimo} — the one that keeps its vowel
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How is an ordinal above ten made? (\textbf{Cardinal, final vowel off, \emph{-esimo} on}.) Say the twentieth. (\textbf{Ventesimo}.) And which number keeps its final vowel? (\emph{\textbf{Tre}} — \emph{ventitreesimo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[prima]{prima — before, which is first in disguise}

\label{lesson:IT-C28-prima}



\begin{quote}
Recalls open the chapter's last stretch, at the four measured distances.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{undicesimo} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{settimo} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{la bocca} — \textbf{R2}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sono andato} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{la testa} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{Come ti chiami?} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{prima} — \textbf{before}, \textbf{earlier}, \textbf{first (of all)}. \textbf{prima di mangiare} — before eating. \textbf{Vengo prima.} — I'll come earlier. \textbf{prima o poi} — sooner or later.
\end{quote}

Before a noun or a verb it takes \textbf{di}: \emph{prima di cena}, \textquotedblleft{}before dinner\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
You have seen this word already, and not as an adverb. \textbf{Prima} is the feminine of \emph{\textbf{primo}}.

Latin froze it in an old case form — \emph{prīmā}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{at the first}\textquotedblright{}, where \textquotedblleft{}the first time\textquotedblright{} was understood and never said — and the frozen phrase became a plain word meaning \textquotedblleft{}before\textquotedblright{}. So Italian's ordinary word for \emph{before} is, underneath, the ordinal for \emph{first}.

Which is a reasonable thing for a language to do: putting one thing before another IS putting it first. English does the same trick from the other direction, using \emph{first} as an adverb — \textquotedblleft{}first, we eat\textquotedblright{} — and never noticing.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{prima} — before, earlier
  \item \emph{prima di cena} — before dinner
  \item \emph{prima} and \emph{prima volta} — the same word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{prima}, taken apart? (\textbf{The feminine of \emph{primo}}, frozen in an old case meaning \textquotedblleft{}at the first\textquotedblright{}.) What does it take before a noun? (\emph{\textbf{Di}} — \emph{prima di cena}.) And say \textquotedblleft{}sooner or later.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Prima o poi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dopo]{dopo — after, and the pair completed}

\label{lesson:IT-C28-dopo}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, then the word that finishes the pair.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{prima} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ottavo} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{il naso} — \textbf{R2}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{la mano} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pensare} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{piacere} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{dopo} — \textbf{after}, \textbf{afterwards}, \textbf{later}. \textbf{dopo cena} — after dinner. \textbf{A dopo!} — See you later. \textbf{dopodomani} — the day after tomorrow.
\end{quote}

Unlike \emph{prima} it takes no \emph{di} before a noun: \emph{dopo cena}, not \emph{dopo di cena}. (Before a pronoun it does: \emph{dopo di me}.)

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Dopo} is two Latin words stuck together: \emph{\textbf{dē}} + \emph{\textbf{post}}, \textquotedblleft{}from after\textquotedblright{}. Latin had \emph{post} on its own; late Latin propped it up with \emph{dē}, the pair fused, and Italian inherited the weld as a single word.

The \emph{post} inside it is the one English keeps in \textbf{postpone} (\textquotedblleft{}to place after\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{post mortem}, \textbf{posterity} and \textbf{post-war} — and in \emph{a.m.} and \emph{p.m.}, where \textbf{p.m.} is \emph{post merīdiem}, \textquotedblleft{}after midday\textquotedblright{}.

With \emph{prima} and \emph{dopo} you can now put two things in order without counting them at all: \emph{prima il primo, dopo il secondo} — first the pasta, then the meat.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dopo} — after, afterwards
  \item \emph{dopo cena} — after dinner
  \item \emph{A dopo!} — see you later
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two Latin words is \emph{dopo} made of? (\emph{\textbf{Dē}} + \emph{\textbf{post}}.) Which everyday abbreviation carries the same \emph{post}? (\textbf{p.m.} — \emph{post merīdiem}.) And what can you do with \emph{prima} and \emph{dopo} that the ordinals do not do for you? (\textbf{Put two things in order} without counting them.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[prima il primo, dopo il secondo]{Putting a meal in order — primo, secondo, prima, dopo}

\label{lesson:IT-C28-practice}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, and then the chapter's work: everything in one place.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dopo} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nono} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{lo stomaco} — \textbf{R2}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{capire} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{leggere} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{the third chapter's own recombining} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the three chapters, on one table}
You have ten ordinals, an ending that makes the rest, and \emph{prima} and \emph{dopo}. That is enough to put things in sequence, and the easiest place to do it is a table.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Prima l'antipasto.} — The antipasto first.
  \item \textbf{Poi il primo.} — Then the first course.
  \item \textbf{Dopo il primo, il secondo.} — After the first, the second.
  \item \textbf{Alla fine, il dolce.} — At the end, the sweet.
\end{itemize}

Two ways of saying the same order, and they do different work. The \textbf{ordinals} name each thing's place — \emph{il primo} is the first, whatever comes near it. \textbf{Prima} and \textbf{dopo} name a relation between two things — \emph{dopo il primo} is true of anything that follows it.

So: \emph{Il caffè viene dopo il dolce} — the coffee comes after the sweet — and \emph{fra un quarto d'ora}, in a quarter of an hour, is how long you might wait for it. Say the courses in order, then say them again with \emph{prima} and \emph{dopo}, and you have used both systems on the same four things.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the courses — \emph{l'antipasto, il primo, il secondo, il dolce}
  \item the relation — \emph{dopo il primo, il secondo}
  \item \emph{il caffè viene dopo il dolce}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the four courses in order. (\textbf{L'antipasto, il primo, il secondo, il dolce}.) What do \emph{prima} and \emph{dopo} do that the ordinals do not? (\textbf{Name a relation between two things}, not each thing's place.) And when does the coffee come? (\emph{\textbf{Dopo il dolce}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
